claim: Dnmt3a is expressed in the entire Keratin-14+ compartment comprising the basal layer of the embryonic epidermis and the hair placodes at E14.5.
source: At E14.5, Dnmt3a was expressed in the entire Keratin-14+ compartment comprising the basal layer of the embryonic epidermis and the hair placodes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At P0, all Keratin-14+ basal cells were positive for Dnmt3a with the exception of the highly proliferative hair follicle bulb cells.
source: At P0, all Keratin-14+ basal cells were positive for Dnmt3a with the exception of the highly proliferative hair follicle bulb cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: In adult animals, Dnmt3a levels remained high in the hair follicle bulge where most hair follicle stem cells reside.
source: By the time animals reached adulthood, Dnmt3a levels remained high in the hair follicle bulge where most hair follicle stem cells reside (Solanas and Benitah, 2013), and decreased in the interfollicular epidermis, although some basal IFE cells expressed high levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-D and cited literature.

claim: Dnmt3a was enriched almost fivefold as compared to Dnmt3b in adult basal IFE keratinocytes.
source: In fact, RNA-seq data confirmed that Dnmt3a was enriched almost fivefold as compared to Dnmt3b in adult basal IFE keratinocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Dnmt1 was the most abundant DNA methyltransferase in both interfollicular epidermis and hair follicle bulge cells.
source: However, Dnmt1, the main DNA methyltransferase, was the most abundant DNA methyltransferase, both in interfollicular epidermis and in hair follicle bulge cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Neither Dnmt3a- nor Dnmt3b-cKO displayed noteworthy epidermal phenotypical differences as compared to their wild-type littermates at different postnatal ages.
source: Surprisingly, neither Dnmt3a- nor Dnmt3b-cKO displayed noteworthy epidermal phenotypical differences as compared to their wild-type littermates at different postnatal ages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Loss of Dnmt3a did not result in evident changes in hair follicle cycling and pelage growth.
source: Likewise, despite its strong expression in hair follicle stem cells, the loss of Dnmt3a did not result in evident changes in hair follicle cycling and pelage growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: The first epidermal squamous malignancies appeared significantly sooner in Dnmt3a-cKO than in their wild-type littermates, after only 2 months from the first DMBA treatment.
source: The first epidermal squamous malignancies appeared significantly sooner in Dnmt3a-cKO than in their wild-type littermates, after only 2 months from the first DMBA treatment, indicating that Dnmt3a acts as a barrier against tumor initiation (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor appearance data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Dnmt3a acts as a barrier against tumor initiation.
source: The first epidermal squamous malignancies appeared significantly sooner in Dnmt3a-cKO than in their wild-type littermates, after only 2 months from the first DMBA treatment, indicating that Dnmt3a acts as a barrier against tumor initiation (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that tumors appear sooner in Dnmt3a-cKO mice.

claim: Dnmt3a-cKO animals showed a significant increase in tumor burden, with an average of 17 tumors per animal compared to three tumors per wild-type animal after 6 months of initiating the experiment.
source: Dnmt3a-cKO animals also showed a significant increase in tumor burden, with an average of 17 tumors per animal compared to three tumors per wild-type animal after 6 months of initiating the experiment (Figure 1C and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor count data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: Dnmt3a-cKO animals developed the same percentage of squamous cell carcinomas as wild-type mice.
source: Although Dnmt3a-cKO animals showed a strong increase in tumor initiation and burden, they developed the same percentage of squamous cell carcinomas than wild-type mice (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by histopathological analysis shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Dnmt3a-cKO mice developed the same percentage of benign tumors, such as keratoacanthomas and papillomas, as well as of malignant invasive papillomas and squamous cell carcinomas as wild-type mice.
source: Indeed, a detailed histological analysis of the tumors collected from Dnmt3a-cKO and wild-type animals indicated that Dnmt3a-cKO mice developed the same percentage of benign tumors, such as keratoacanthomas and papillomas, as well as of malignant invasive papillomas and squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs) (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by histopathological analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Dnmt3a-cKO mice only developed an increase in the percentage of sebaceous adenomas.
source: Dnmt3a-cKO mice only developed an increase in the percentage of sebaceous adenomas (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by histopathological analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: No metastases were scored in any of the animals using the DMBA/TPA protocol in mice with a C57/Bl6 genetic background.
source: No metastases were scored in any of the animals, as expected using this protocol in mice with a C57/Bl6 genetic background (Sundberg et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by the absence of metastases in the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: Loss of Dnmt3a dramatically increases initiation of epidermal squamous tumors without affecting their malignant progression.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that loss of Dnmt3a dramatically increases initiation of epidermal squamous tumors without affecting their malignant progression, and slightly skews the histology of tumors towards the sebaceous lineage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of increased tumor initiation but similar progression rates.

claim: There were no differences between wild-type and Dnmt3b-cKO mice with respect to either the timing of tumor initiation or tumor burden upon treatment with DMBA/TPA.
source: Interestingly, there were no differences between wild-type and Dnmt3b-cKO mice with respect to either the timing of tumor initiation or tumor burden upon treatment with DMBA/TPA (Figure 2A-right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor appearance and burden data shown in Figure 2A-right panel.

claim: There were no significant changes in the histological appearance of the tumors, or the number of basal cells proliferating or undergoing apoptosis, between Dnmt3b-cKO and the wild-type controls.
source: There were no significant changes in the histological appearance of the tumors, or the number of basal cells proliferating or undergoing apoptosis, between Dnmt3b-cKO and the wild-type controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological and immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: DcKO animals displayed a significantly shortened latency and significant higher tumor burden than wild-type mice.
source: Strikingly, although DcKO animals had a severe depletion of DNA methylation in their epidermises, they formed a morphologically normal skin with all its appendages and did not develop any epidermal abnormality even up to 70 weeks of age (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–B). This strongly suggests that de novo DNA methylation is dispensable for the long-term homeostasis of undamaged epidermis. However, when subjected to tumorigenesis, DcKO animals displayed a significantly shortened latency and significant higher tumor burden than wild-type mice (Figure 2B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor appearance and burden data shown in Figure 2B-F.

claim: De novo DNA methylation is dispensable for the long-term homeostasis of undamaged epidermis.
source: Strikingly, although DcKO animals had a severe depletion of DNA methylation in their epidermises, they formed a morphologically normal skin with all its appendages and did not develop any epidermal abnormality even up to 70 weeks of age (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–B). This strongly suggests that de novo DNA methylation is dispensable for the long-term homeostasis of undamaged epidermis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that DcKO animals have normal skin despite severe DNA methylation depletion.

claim: DcKO mice formed aggressive squamous cell carcinomas at a higher frequency as compared to the single cKOs of Dnmt3a or Dnmt3b.
source: Although these differences were similar to the ones observed in single Dnmt3a-cKO mice (Figure 2C–D), DcKO mice formed aggressive squamous cell carcinomas at a higher frequency as compared to the single cKOs of Dnmt3a or Dnmt3b (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by histopathological analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Metastatic nodules in the lungs were observed in 30% of DcKO animals, but in none of the wild-type, Dnmt3a-cKO, or Dnmt3b-cKO animals.
source: In addition, metastatic nodules in the lungs were observed in 30% of DcKO animals, but in none of the wild-type, Dnmt3a-cKO, or Dnmt3b-cKO animals (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: DcKO tumors contained large areas with spindle-shaped cells that expressed lower levels of the epithelial markers E-Cadherin and Keratin14, compared to the wild type and to Dnmt3a-cKO tumors.
source: Interestingly, DcKO tumors contained large areas with spindle-shaped cells that expressed lower levels of the epithelial markers E-Cadherin and Keratin14, compared to the wild type and to Dnmt3a-cKO tumors (Figure 2E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Spindle-shaped cells in DcKO tumors expressed the mesenchymal marker Vimentin.
source: These cells also expressed the mesenchymal marker Vimentin (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6A-C.

claim: Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b are dispensable for epidermal homeostasis.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b are dispensable for epidermal homeostasis, and that Dnmt3a, but not Dnmt3b, suppresses skin squamous tumor initiation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that knockout animals have normal skin homeostasis.

claim: Dnmt3a, but not Dnmt3b, suppresses skin squamous tumor initiation.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b are dispensable for epidermal homeostasis, and that Dnmt3a, but not Dnmt3b, suppresses skin squamous tumor initiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the differential tumor initiation phenotypes observed in Dnmt3a-cKO versus Dnmt3b-cKO mice.

claim: Both Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b repress the malignant transformation of epidermal cells into aggressive squamous cell carcinomas.
source: However, both Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b repress the malignant transformation of epidermal cells into aggressive squamous cell carcinomas.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that DcKO mice develop more aggressive tumors than single knockouts.

claim: 391 genes were consistently differentially expressed between wild-type and Dnmt3a-cKO tumors, of which 114 were downregulated and 277 were upregulated in the latter.
source: Nevertheless, 391 genes were consistently differentially expressed between wild-type and Dnmt3a-cKO tumors, of which 114 were downregulated and 277 were upregulated in the latter (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The downregulated genes in Dnmt3a-cKO tumors were mainly associated with apoptosis.
source: The downregulated genes were mainly associated with apoptosis, suggesting that loss of Dnmt3a promotes cell survival and protects against programmed cell death (Figure 3D)
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Dnmt3a-cKO tumors had fewer apoptotic cells as compared to wild-type tumors.
source: consequently, TUNEL and active Caspase3 staining confirmed that Dnmt3a-cKO tumors had fewer apoptotic cells as compared to wild-type tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2—Source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL and Caspase3 staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Dnmt3a-cKO tumors expressed higher levels of several genes involved in cell proliferation.
source: Dnmt3a-cKO tumors also expressed higher levels of several genes involved in cell proliferation (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Proliferation was only significantly increased in pre-cancerous DMBA/TPA-treated Dnmt3a-cKO epidermis.
source: Interestingly, proliferation was only significantly increased in pre-cancerous DMBA/TPA-treated Dnmt3a-cKO epidermis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–B), while no differences in proliferation were evident between the homeostatic epidermis and tumors of wild-type and Dnmt3a-cKO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by KI67 staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: The loss of Dnmt3a endows pre-cancerous mutant basal cells with a survival and proliferative advantage.
source: Altogether, this suggests that the loss of Dnmt3a endows pre-cancerous mutant basal cells with a survival and proliferative advantage, which could account for the increased number of tumors these mice develop.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of increased proliferation and decreased apoptosis in pre-cancerous tissue.

claim: Two principal pathways were over-represented in all eight Dnmt3a-cKO tumors: Wnt signaling and lipid metabolism.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of the 277 genes that were upregulated in Dnmt3a-cKO basal tumor cells highlighted two principal pathways that were over-represented in all eight Dnmt3a-cKO tumors: Wnt signaling (including ligands and receptors), and more predominantly, lipid metabolism (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The most upregulated genes in Dnmt3a-cKO tumors encoded the key pro-adipogenic transcription factors PPAR-α and PPAR-γ.
source: Among these, the most upregulated ones encoded the key pro-adipogenic transcription factors PPAR-α and PPAR-γ, which promote adipocyte differentiation and the expression of genes involved in fatty acid metabolism, and which are not expressed in homeostatic epidermal cells (Fajas et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and cited literature.

claim: PPAR-γ was upregulated at the RNA and protein levels in all the Dnmt3a-cKO sequenced tumors.
source: Importantly, PPAR-γ was upregulated at the RNA and protein levels in all the Dnmt3a-cKO sequenced tumors (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A-B.

claim: Most of the upregulated genes in epidermal cells (IFE) after short DMBA/TPA treatment were predominantly linked to lipid metabolism and cell proliferation.
source: After this short DMBA/TPA treatment, most of the upregulated genes in epidermal cells (IFE) were already predominantly linked to lipid metabolism and cell proliferation, whereas they related mostly to cell proliferation, and Wnt signaling in bulge stem cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: 16,483 genomic locations were bound by Dnmt3a in wild-type animals, but only 64 in Dnmt3a-cKO.
source: We detected 16,483 genomic locations bound by Dnmt3a in wild-type animals, but only 64 in Dnmt3a-cKO, confirming the specificity of the Dnmt3a antibody (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: More than 20% of Dnmt3a-bound regions corresponded to intergenic regions.
source: Of the bound regions in the wild-type epidermis, more than 20% corresponded to intergenic regions (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 10% of active enhancers were bound by Dnmt3a in wild-type cells.
source: ChIP-Seq for H3K27ac using the same samples allowed us to identify 3097 intergenic regions enriched for H3K27ac that corresponded to active enhancers, 10% of which were bound by Dnmt3a in wild-type cells (Figure 4A–C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A-C and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The active enhancers bound by Dnmt3a predominantly corresponded to genes essential for keratinocyte differentiation and transcriptional regulation.
source: Interestingly, proximity-based analysis revealed that the active enhancers bound by Dnmt3a predominantly corresponded to genes essential for keratinocyte differentiation and transcriptional regulation, such as Evpl (encoding for Envoplakin), Ppl (encoding for Periplakin), Fos, Myc, Cebpa, and Fosl2 (Figure 4C–D), similarly to what we have previously reported in human epidermal keratinocytes (Rinaldi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4C-D and cited literature.

claim: The active enhancers bound by Dnmt3a contained higher levels of DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation than those not bound by it.
source: The active enhancers bound by Dnmt3a contained higher levels of DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation than those not bound by it (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeDIP-seq and hMeDIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A,C.

claim: Loss of Dnmt3a significantly reduced DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation at active enhancers bound by Dnmt3a.
source: Importantly, loss of Dnmt3a significantly reduced their DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeDIP-seq and hMeDIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A,C.

claim: A significant reduction in DNA methylation occurred in enhancers not bound by Dnmt3a upon deletion of Dnmt3a, albeit to a statistically significantly lesser extent than those directly targeted by Dnmt3a in wild-type cells.
source: Intriguingly, a significant reduction in DNA methylation also occurred in enhancers not bound by Dnmt3a, albeit to a statistically significantly lesser extent than those directly targeted by Dnmt3a in wild-type cells (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeDIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The presence of Dnmt3a correlates with significantly higher 5-hmC levels.
source: However, the ratio of 5-hmC levels at enhancers bound by Dnmt3a between wild-type and Dnmt3a-cKO epidermal cells is significantly higher as compared to the ratio of 5-hmC levels between the enhancers that are not normally bound by Dnmt3a (Figure 5D). This indicates that the presence of Dnmt3a correlates with significantly higher 5-hmC levels, likely because Dnmt3a provides 5-mC as a substrate for generating 5-hmC, as we have previously shown in human keratinocytes (Rinaldi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the ratio of 5-hmC levels shown in Figure 5D and cited literature.

claim: 19% of the enriched regions for Dnmt3a corresponded to promoters/TSSs.
source: In addition to active enhancers, a significant proportion (19%) of the enriched regions for Dnmt3a corresponded to promoters/TSSs (Figure 4B and Supplement file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The promoters bound by Dnmt3a showed a strong and statistically significant loss of DNA methylation around the corresponding TSS.
source: Notably, the promoters bound by Dnmt3a showed a strong and statistically significant loss of DNA methylation around the corresponding TSS (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeDIP-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The levels of DNA methylation were not significantly changed at promoters not bound by Dnmt3a.
source: The levels of DNA methylation were not significantly changed at promoters not bound by Dnmt3a (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeDIP-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The loss of DNA methylation at the promoters/TSSs bound by Dnmt3a was accompanied by a general increase in the transcription of these genes.
source: The loss of DNA methylation at the promoters/TSSs bound by Dnmt3a was also accompanied by a general increase in the transcription of these genes, measured by RNA-seq in the tumors (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Dnmt3a directly represses the expression of a specific subset of genes by methylating their promoters/TSSs.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that Dnmt3a directly represses the expression of a specific subset of genes by methylating their promoters/TSSs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of Dnmt3a binding, DNA methylation, and gene expression changes.

claim: The promoters bound by Dnmt3a regulated the expression of genes predominantly involved in cell proliferation and lipid metabolism.
source: Interestingly, a GO analysis of the promoters bound by Dnmt3a indicated that they regulated the expression of genes predominantly involved in cell proliferation and lipid metabolism, consistent with our RNA-seq results (Figure 6D and Supplement file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 6D and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Dnmt3a bound the promoters of Ppar-α and Ppar-γ in wild-type but not Dnmt3a-cKO epidermis.
source: Interestingly, Dnmt3a bound the promoters of Ppar-α and Ppar-γ in wild-type but not Dnmt3a-cKO epidermis (Figure 6E and Supplement file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6E and Supplementary file 3.

claim: 5-mC levels were lower in the TSS of the PPAR-γ gene in Dnmt3a-cKO as compared to wild-type tumors.
source: Furthermore, 5-mC levels were lower in the TSS of the PPAR-γ gene in Dnmt3a-cKO as compared to wild-type tumors, indicating a DNA methylation-dependent mechanism of transcriptional repression (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by MeDIP-seq data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: PPAR-γ mRNA and protein levels were upregulated both in pre-cancerous interfollicular epidermis and in tumors lacking Dnmt3a.
source: Consistent with a transcriptional derepression of the locus following loss of DNA methylation, PPAR-γ mRNA and protein levels were upregulated both in pre-cancerous interfollicular epidermis and in tumors lacking Dnmt3a, suggesting that the upregulation of PPAR-γ is acquired at the pre-cancerous stage, even before overt tumors appear (Figure 6G,H and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6G,H and Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: Inhibition of PPAR-γ significantly delayed the onset of tumor appearance in Dnmt3a-cKO mice.
source: Interestingly, inhibition of PPAR-γ significantly delayed the onset of tumor appearance in Dnmt3a-cKO mice, and reduced the number of tumors developed by the Dnmt3a-cKO (Figure 7B–C and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor appearance data shown in Figure 7B-C and Figure 7—source data 1.

claim: Inhibition of PPAR-γ reduced the number of tumors developed by Dnmt3a-cKO mice.
source: Interestingly, inhibition of PPAR-γ significantly delayed the onset of tumor appearance in Dnmt3a-cKO mice, and reduced the number of tumors developed by the Dnmt3a-cKO (Figure 7B–C and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor count data shown in Figure 7B-C and Figure 7—source data 1.

claim: The average size of the tumors was not affected by the inhibition of PPAR-γ.
source: However, the average size of the tumors was not affected by the inhibition of PPAR-γ (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor size data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Inhibition of PPAR-γ could be a potential new therapy for cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas harboring low levels of Dnmt3a.
source: Thus, inhibition of PPAR-γ could be a potential new therapy for cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas harboring low levels of Dnmt3a.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed effects of PPAR-γ inhibition in the mouse model.

claim: The expression of Dnmt3a is significantly reduced in squamous cell carcinomas and actinic keratosis compared to human healthy epidermis.
source: At last, using public available data from four different studies we determined that the expression of Dnmt3a is significantly reduced in squamous cell carcinomas and actinic keratosis, the premalignant stage of squamous tumors, compared to human healthy epidermis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1—Source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of publicly available data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1—Source data 1.

claim: Dnmt3a suppresses tumorigenesis in models of leukemia and lung cancer.
source: The DNA methyltransferase Dnmt3a suppresses tumorigenesis in models of leukemia and lung cancer.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Deregulation of Dnmt3b is thought to generally promote tumorigenesis.
source: Conversely, deregulation of Dnmt3b is thought to generally promote tumorigenesis.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Loss of Dnmt3a increases the number of carcinogen-induced squamous tumors, without affecting tumor progression.
source: However, loss of Dnmt3a-but not Dnmt3b-increases the number of carcinogen-induced squamous tumors, without affecting tumor progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor count and progression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only upon combined deletion of Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b, squamous carcinomas become more aggressive and metastatic.
source: Only upon combined deletion of Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b, squamous carcinomas become more aggressive and metastatic.
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor histology and metastasis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dnmt3a promotes the expression of epidermal differentiation genes by interacting with their enhancers.
source: Mechanistically, Dnmt3a promotes the expression of epidermal differentiation genes by interacting with their enhancers and inhibits the expression of lipid metabolism genes, including PPAR-γ, by directly methylating their promoters.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq and gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dnmt3a inhibits the expression of lipid metabolism genes, including PPAR-γ, by directly methylating their promoters.
source: Mechanistically, Dnmt3a promotes the expression of epidermal differentiation genes by interacting with their enhancers and inhibits the expression of lipid metabolism genes, including PPAR-γ, by directly methylating their promoters.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq, MeDIP-seq, and gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition of PPAR-γ partially prevents the increase in tumorigenesis upon deletion of Dnmt3a.
source: Importantly, inhibition of PPAR-γ partially prevents the increase in tumorigenesis upon deletion of Dnmt3a.
evidence: The claim is supported by tumor count data from PPAR-γ inhibitor experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b protect the epidermis from tumorigenesis.
source: Altogether, we demonstrate that Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b protect the epidermis from tumorigenesis and that squamous carcinomas are sensitive to inhibition of PPAR-γ.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of increased tumorigenesis in knockout mice.

claim: Squamous carcinomas are sensitive to inhibition of PPAR-γ.
source: Altogether, we demonstrate that Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b protect the epidermis from tumorigenesis and that squamous carcinomas are sensitive to inhibition of PPAR-γ.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observed effects of PPAR-γ inhibition on tumor development.

claim: DNA methylation is an epigenetic mechanism that regulates several aspects of gene expression, such as long-term gene silencing, transcriptional elongation, and maintenance of genomic stability.
source: DNA methylation is an epigenetic mechanism that regulates several aspects of gene expression, such as long-term gene silencing, transcriptional elongation, and maintenance of genomic stability (Allis and Jenuwein, 2016; Avgustinova and Benitah, 2016; Rinaldi and Benitah, 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Dnmt1 is predominantly associated with the maintenance of DNA methylation following cell division due to its high affinity for hemimethylated DNA.
source: Dnmt1 is predominantly associated with the maintenance of DNA methylation following cell division due to its high affinity for hemimethylated DNA.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Depletion of Dnmt1 leads to a significant reduction of the global levels of 5-mC.
source: Consequently, depletion of Dnmt1 leads to a significant reduction of the global levels of 5-mC (Li et al., 1992; Lei et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b are de novo DNA methyltransferases that establish genome-wide DNA methylation during mammalian embryogenesis and adult stem cell homeostasis.
source: Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b are de novo DNA methyltransferases that establish genome-wide DNA methylation during mammalian embryogenesis and adult stem cell homeostasis (Okano et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The combined loss of Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b in mouse embryonic stem cells leads to the progressive loss of DNA methylation.
source: In mouse embryonic stem cells, the combined loss of Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b leads to the progressive loss of DNA methylation, suggesting that these enzymes are additionally involved in maintaining 5-mC levels (Chen et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) lacking Dnmt3a cannot differentiate correctly upon serial transplantation, and end up developing a range of severe myeloid and lymphoid malignancies in aged animals.
source: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) lacking Dnmt3a cannot differentiate correctly upon serial transplantation, and end up developing a range of severe myeloid and lymphoid malignancies in aged animals (Challen et al., 2011; Mayle et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: HSCs-depleted of Dnmt3b show no phenotypical differences with respect to wild-type controls.
source: Conversely, HSCs-depleted of Dnmt3b show no phenotypical differences with respect to wild-type controls, whereas combined ablation of Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b in HSCs result in an enhanced block of hematopoietic differentiation as compared to Dnmt3a loss alone (Challen et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Combined ablation of Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b in HSCs result in an enhanced block of hematopoietic differentiation as compared to Dnmt3a loss alone.
source: Conversely, HSCs-depleted of Dnmt3b show no phenotypical differences with respect to wild-type controls, whereas combined ablation of Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b in HSCs result in an enhanced block of hematopoietic differentiation as compared to Dnmt3a loss alone (Challen et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Fully differentiated cardiac myocytes carrying a combined deletion of Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b are indistinguishable from wild-type controls.
source: Interestingly, the observed phenotype seems specific to stem cells, as the fully differentiated cardiac myocytes carrying a combined deletion of Dnmt3a and Dnmt3b are indistinguishable from wild-type controls (Nührenberg et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Purified murine neural stem cells (SCs) lacking Dnmt3a do not show problems with self-renewal but fail to differentiate properly.
source: Similarly, to HSCs, purified murine neural stem cells (SCs) lacking Dnmt3a do not show problems with self-renewal but fail to differentiate properly (Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Dnmt3a acts as a potent tumor suppressor in lung tumorigenesis, to promote adenoma progression but not initiation, downstream of oncogenic K-Ras.
